fr:mainmatter.html:p: A universal element of a presheaf P on a category C is an element x \in P c, where c is some object of C, demonstrating that P is representable by c.

(Slightly) more concretely, a universal element is captured by the following three pieces of data
An object c of C
An element x \in P c
A proof that the map sending a morphism f : b \to c to (Pf)(x) is an equivalence
This third point states that morphisms from b into c are uniquely determined by an element of P at the domain b.
Or equivalently, universal elements are terminal in the category of elements.

fr:title.text: What is a universal property, really?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What is a universal property, really?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Universal properties are a convenient method for defining an object in a category up to isomorphism. Rather than giving a concrete, bottom-up construction of an object, we can instead uniquely specify its behavior.

Surely this matches our set-based intuition of what a product should behave like. Similarly, we can sketch out constructions of other universal properties like initial objects, terminal objects, exponentials, etc. However, what is precisely meant by the term universal property?

The notion of a universal property is made precise by the notion of a universal element of a presheaf. That is, an object satisfies a universal property if we can build a universal element of the appropriate presheaf at that object.

Let's look at the universal element characterization of the products example. Note that a map into a product is determined by a map into each component. To map into c \times d, we need both a map into c and a map into d, as in the above diagram. That is, to build a map b \to c \times d, we must simultaneously provide elements of よ c and よ d at b.

Using the product of presheaves, this means we are providing a single element of the presheaf (よ c) \times (よ d). Quite nicely, the universal element of this presheaf provides the object of C that is the product of c and d. The universal element, provided that it exists, contains the following data:
An object p
An element x \in (よ c \times よ d) p
A proof that the map sending f : b \to p to a pair of maps f_1 : b \to c, f_2 : b \to d is an equivlance. Therefore, any element of よ c \times よ d factors through x
Recall that the product of presheaves is computed pointwise in the category of sets, so if we expand the type of the element x above we find that x is a pair of maps p \to c and p \to d.
(よ c \times よ d) p \cong (よ c p) \times (よ d p)
The first part of this pair is precisely \pi _1. Correspondingly, the second part of this pair is \pi _2. Finally, the universality of the element x (i.e. the proof that any other element factors through x) captures our commutative diagram from above.

This is a very rough sketch of what a universal property is, and has elided for now an important application of the Yoneda lemma. In any cases, all a univeral property is really saying is that a particular presheaf is representable; and, rather elegantly, a universal element of a presheaf is convenient packaging of that representability proof.

In summary, universal properties are not as ad-hoc as they may initially seem, and the language of presheaves provides a reusable and precise definition that can be instantiated to describe a very large class of properties.
